# A finite actual obstruction to diagonal spectral quasiconvexity

This note disproves an unrestricted deformation shortcut. It does not
disprove the planar cubic inequality, and the example does not satisfy
the small-cap ceiling used in the mixed-integer application.

Use the balanced normals `(1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)` at the origin. For
`9/10 <= t <= 11/10`, let the counterclockwise quadrilateral be

    K_t=conv{(7-17t,-6+15t),(1,-5),(7,-6),(2,4)}.

Thus three vertices stay fixed and the fourth moves along its diagonal
through the opposite vertex `(7,-6)`. Every successive edge determinant
and every oriented edge-to-origin determinant is positive throughout
this interval: these determinants are affine in t, so it suffices to
check the two endpoints. Hence every K_t is a convex quadrilateral with
the same cyclic vertex order and the origin strictly inside it. Each
vertex has the same strict sign against each of the three normals
throughout the interval, again by affine endpoint checking. No cutting
line passes through a vertex or changes its clipping incidence.

Let k be area, Q_i the three captured areas, sigma_i the normalized cut
lengths, and

    M=sum_i Q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=2 sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i M).

Let B(f) have zero diagonal and successive off-diagonal entries f_i/2.
The cubic spectral objective is its largest eigenvalue J. The exact
clipping data at three parameters are:

| t | k | (Q_1,Q_2,Q_3) | (sigma_1,sigma_2,sigma_3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9/10 | 378/5 | (785623/19158,423/10,2672/85) | (79846/9579,168/25,2191/170) |
| 1 | 84 | (2719/66,1405/28,2537/70) | (565/66,97/14,493/35) |
| 11/10 | 462/5 | (1438503/34798,18029/310,165/4) | (151866/17399,220/31,913/60) |

Here the normalized length for the third normal is the absolute change
in the x coordinate between the two cut endpoints; this equals Euclidean
length divided by sqrt(2). The other two normalized lengths are the
corresponding vertical and horizontal changes.

Set r=9353/10000. All quantities f_i^2 are rational. Write

    S=sum_i f_i^2, P2=product_i f_i^2, A=4r^3-rS.

At all three parameters A>0 and r^2>max_i f_i^2/4. Exact substitution of
the displayed data gives A^2-P2 positive at t=9/10 and t=11/10, but
negative at t=1. For an independently reproducible integer certificate,
the numerators of these reduced rational differences, in that order, are

    3510706410588836264660605017721653291756515117813998422666165627020123424388441,
    -540700198098510021635901969811763587528417542044536772194256639,
    9199865969993839138293812145495142011729826509614410900268826474431000361.

Indeed

    det(r I-B(f))=(A-sqrt(P2))/4.

At the two endpoints the positive first and second principal minors and
this positive determinant prove rI-B positive definite. At the middle
parameter its negative determinant prevents positive semidefiniteness.
Consequently

    J(K_(9/10)) < r < J(K_1),
    J(K_(11/10)) < r < J(K_1).

Continuity therefore gives an attained maximum strictly inside the
parameter interval. In particular the spectral objective is not
quasiconvex along every fixed-incidence diagonal deformation, even when
every body and every cut remain strictly nondegenerate.

All three displayed bodies satisfy the cubic inequality strictly:
`4-S>0` and `(4-S)^2>P2` verify this without numerical eigenvalues.
Therefore this example leaves open a deformation principle restricted
to a hypothetical cubic-violating level or to a suitable small-cap band.
It rules out only the unrestricted no-interior-maximum statement.

The companion
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_diagonal_quad_spectral_peak_defect_transport.py` performs all
geometry, clipping, and characteristic-polynomial comparisons using
exact rational arithmetic; its 33 checks pass.
